description: We are a team of Korean middle and high school students taking on the 2026 challenge Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions. Our interests are software development, data analysis, and applying open NASA data to real problems in human spaceflight. We are participating online. Our team is complete, but we welcome conversations with other participants and subject-matter experts.
summary:
SpaceVital47 is an AI-powered astronaut health monitoring system designed for long-duration space missions. It combines real-time vital sign monitoring, daily health self-assessments, and camera-based facial analysis to track astronauts' health and detect potential abnormalities early. By comparing current data with personal health records, it identifies unusual changes and monitors health trends over time.

In emergencies, SpaceVital47 provides mission control with quick access to astronauts' health information, enabling faster and better-informed medical decisions. Its ultimate goal is to support early detection, continuous health monitoring, and reliable medical care when immediate medical assistance from Earth is impossible.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

SpaceVital47 is a browser-based health monitor for astronauts. A crew member does a one-to-three minute daily self-check: a few numbers (heart rate, temperature, sleep, stress, food intake, exercise, cabin CO2), then structured symptom modules (12 modules, with red-flag symptoms marked). The app compares today with yesterday and with the person's own baseline, in a vital-monitor layout. Levels use stars and icons, never color alone. Missing days break the line; the app never fills gaps with fake data.

When a serious trigger appears, the app switches to one of 13 step-by-step emergency cards (for example allergic reaction, infection getting worse, eye injury, radiation shelter). It switches only for a new trigger, so it does not nag. It also writes a ready-to-send English report for the ground team, and the steps change if there is no link to the ground.

An optional camera layer measures change in skin redness in a few regions (forehead, cheeks, eye area, lips). It is only a secondary signal. It checks lighting, glare and position first and asks for a retake if quality is poor. Camera alone can raise a warning but can never trigger an emergency card.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Astronauts are not doctors, and real-time medical help gets harder the farther they travel. The goal is to help a crew member notice small changes early, decide what to do next, and talk to the ground team clearly. Because it works only against the person's own baseline, it does not need one "normal" for everyone.

HOW IT IS BUILT

Plain HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript, no framework, no build step, no server. Everything runs in the browser and sends no data over the network (enforced by a Content Security Policy). It uses the browser camera, canvas and local storage, and is hosted on GitHub Pages. We tested with Node and Playwright: 100 documented measurement cases, 99 automated and passing, 1 manual. Code and data were drafted with Claude (Anthropic) and reviewed by our team.

DATA AND EVIDENCE

The condition list comes from NASA's Integrated Medical Model tables and NASA Human Research Program risk pages. The app also uses NOAA space weather scales and published studies. Every rule must cite a source the team actually read, or it is not loaded. An Evidence tab shows the source and the strength of evidence for each condition and rule, and lists features we dropped because evidence was missing (for example camera drowsiness or stroke detection). All crew data in the demo is synthetic.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

The app treats uncertainty as a feature. It shows what it does not know, refuses to diagnose, and limits what the camera is allowed to do. The daily view is built around change from yourself, not population thresholds.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Privacy (on-device only, consent before camera, delete-all button), alarm fatigue, color accessibility, offline use, and honest limits. All thresholds are demo values. The camera is unvalidated in spaceflight and was tested only with synthetic video. This is a prototype, not a medical device.
